"竹内栖凤的《班猫》与速水御舟的《红梅·白梅》，是馆长山崎妙子在“Ⅰ”的展品中特意选出的自己“心仪”的3件作品之一。《班猫》是该馆学艺部顾问、明治学院大学教授山下裕二在展览图录中评价为〈作为描绘猫的近代日本画达到了最高成就〉的作品。《红梅·白梅》则是妙子馆长小时候坐在祖父种二先生膝盖上观赏过的作品。上村松园、松篁母子是种二交好的画家。特别是松园的作品，据称深受妙子馆长的祖母、也就是种二先生夫人的格外喜爱。", "种二先生在刚开始收藏美术品时，似乎曾买过一幅假的“酒井抱一挂轴”。当时他觉得“以信誉为第一的商人如果装饰了赝品，也会牵连到生意的信誉”，自此之后，他便前往各种展览会培养眼光，并通过众多画商与画家们交流，建立起直接委托作品等关系。前文提到的横山大观曾有一段时间滞留在种二先生位于热海的别墅，而当松园母子从京都来到东京时，他还负责安排住宿和餐饮等事宜。小林古径也是与之有交流的作家之一。以道成寺传说为基础创作的《清姬》是一组自发表以来就评价极高的连作，但与《心神》一样，据说也是因为“如果要建美术馆”才被允许购得的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "山口蓬春的《新宫殿杉戸枫4分之1草图》。对于曾负责皇宫正殿松之间、东走廊杉户画的蓬春，种二向其委托了同类题材的作品，但由于生病创作进展缓慢，该草图于1970年10月在该馆的“日本四季”展上展出。对于英年早逝的速水御舟，种二虽然没有直接交流，但对其作品深怀敬意，这促成了1976年对“安宅收藏”的整体收购。《昆虫二题》是继1925年绘制的重要文化财《炎舞》之后创作的同感之作，光与暗、静与动的对比令人印象深刻。", "山种美术馆在1971～1997年间每两年举办一次“山种美术馆奖”。自2016（平成28）年起定期举办公募展“Seed山种美术馆日本画奖”。亦致力于发掘和培养年轻作家。将这些成果与全新创作的作品一同展出的“Ⅱ”，可以说展现了日本画的当下或对未来的展望。反过来说，本次的“Ⅰ”则是呈现了近代日本画的足迹及其硕果。首先欣赏这部分“Ⅰ”，将有助于更好地欣赏“Ⅱ”。从这个意义上说，这也是一个应当细细品味的展览，笔者不禁如此感叹。（田中聪）", "「ザ・ベスト・オブ・山種コレクションⅠ」は、東京・恵比寿にある山種美術館の「開館60周年記念特別展」の第３弾である。「ザ・ベスト・オブ・山種コレクション」は文字通り、1800点に及ぶ所蔵品の中から「ベスト」を展示するものであり、開催中の「Ⅰ」は旧蔵作品のアンソロジー、12月12日から来年3月7日にかけて開かれる「Ⅱ」は、同館が開催してきた美術賞の受賞作品や、山口晃、福田美蘭ら現代作家に依頼した描き下ろし作品が主体になる。本卦還りを迎えた日本画専門の美術館、その原点や歴史、コンセプトを改めて振り返る企画だといえるだろう。"}, "展覧会は〈第１章 ザ・ベスト・オブ・山種コレクション〉〈第２章 山﨑種二と日本画家〉の２章で構成されている。６点の重要文化財、14点の重要美術品を所蔵する山種美術館。この展覧会では、それらの中から約40点が展示されている。冒頭に挙げた《心神》は、美術館を創立した山﨑種二と懇意だった横山大観の作品。展覧会図録によると、大観から「ひとつ世の中のためになるようなこともやっておいてはどうですか」と勧められたことが、種二氏が美術館を設立するきっかけのひとつになったそうで、《心神》は美術館設立を条件に購入できたのだそうだ。"}, "菱田春草、下村観山、村上華岳、福田平八郎……そうそうたる作家たちのそうそうたる作品が並ぶコレクション。これもまた展覧会図録によれば、〈種二は「特定の流派や画家に限らず、株と同じように分散」する方針で、「画家の人格をみて集め」た〉のだという。〈絵画に関しては、投資の意味もあったが、売買して儲けようとしたことはなかった〉種二は、〈あくまでも自らが楽しむ目的で日本画を購入した〉のである。"}, "竹内栖鳳の《班猫》と速水御舟の《紅梅・白梅》は、山﨑妙子館長が「Ⅰ」の展示品のなかから、あえて自分の「推し」３作に入れた作品。《班猫》は同館学芸部顧問で明治学院大学教授の山下裕二氏が〈猫を描いた近代日本画として最高の達成だと思う〉と展覧会図録で述べている作品。《紅梅・白梅》は、妙子館長が祖父・種二氏のひざに乗せられて見ていた作品だという。上村松園・松篁親子は、種二が懇意にしていた画家。特に松園の作品は、妙子館長の祖母、つまり種二氏の夫人が特に愛好していたという。"}, "種二氏は、美術品収集を始めたころ、偽物の「酒井抱一の掛軸」を買ってしまったことがあったそうだ。そのときに「信用を第一とする商人が贋物を飾っていては、商売の信用にもかかわる」と思い、以降、各種展覧会に足を運んで目を養うとともに、多くの画商を通じて画家たちと交流し、直接作品を依頼するなどの関係になったという。前述した大観は、一時期、熱海の種二氏の別荘に滞在していたし、松園親子が京都から東京に来た際には、宿泊や食事などのアテンドをしていた。小林古径も交流のあった作家のひとり。道成寺伝説をもとにした《清姫》は発表当時から評価が高かった連作だが、《心神》と同様、「美術館を作るのであれば」ということで購入を許されたのだという。"}, article_text:
開館60周年記念特別展3「ザ・ベスト・オブ・山種コレクションⅠ ―横山大観、竹内栖鳳から上村松園、速水御舟へ―」

会場：山種美術館（東京都渋谷区広尾３-１２-３６）

会期：２０２６年１０月１０日（土）～１２月６日（日）

休館日：月曜休館。ただし１１月２３日は開館し、１１月２４日が休館

開館時間：１０：００～１７：００。入場は閉館３０分前まで

入館料：一般１５００円、高校生・大学生１２００円、中学生以下無料（付添者の同伴が必要）

アクセス：JR恵比寿駅西口、東京メトロ日比谷線恵比寿駅２番出口から約１０分

※画像で紹介した作品は、特に記述がない限り、すべて山種美術館所蔵 ※詳細情報は、 公式サイト で確認を

「ザ・ベスト・オブ・山種コレクションⅠ」は、東京・恵比寿にある山種美術館の「開館60周年記念特別展」の第３弾である。「ザ・ベスト・オブ・山種コレクション」は文字通り、1800点に及ぶ所蔵品の中から「ベスト」を展示するものであり、開催中の「Ⅰ」は旧蔵作品のアンソロジー、12月12日から来年3月7日にかけて開かれる「Ⅱ」は、同館が開催してきた美術賞の受賞作品や、山口晃、福田美蘭ら現代作家に依頼した描き下ろし作品が主体になる。本卦還りを迎えた日本画専門の美術館、その原点や歴史、コンセプトを改めて振り返る企画だといえるだろう。

展覧会は〈第１章 ザ・ベスト・オブ・山種コレクション〉〈第２章 山﨑種二と日本画家〉の２章で構成されている。６点の重要文化財、14点の重要美術品を所蔵する山種美術館。この展覧会では、それらの中から約40点が展示されている。冒頭に挙げた《心神》は、美術館を創立した山﨑種二と懇意だった横山大観の作品。展覧会図録によると、大観から「ひとつ世の中のためになるようなこともやっておいてはどうですか」と勧められたことが、種二氏が美術館を設立するきっかけのひとつになったそうで、《心神》は美術館設立を条件に購入できたのだそうだ。

菱田春草、下村観山、村上華岳、福田平八郎……そうそうたる作家たちのそうそうたる作品が並ぶコレクション。これもまた展覧会図録によれば、〈種二は「特定の流派や画家に限らず、株と同じように分散」する方針で、「画家の人格をみて集め」た〉のだという。〈絵画に関しては、投資の意味もあったが、売買して儲けようとしたことはなかった〉種二は、〈あくまでも自らが楽しむ目的で日本画を購入した〉のである。

竹内栖鳳の《班猫》と速水御舟の《紅梅・白梅》は、山﨑妙子館長が「Ⅰ」の展示品のなかから、あえて自分の「推し」３作に入れた作品。《班猫》は同館学芸部顧問で明治学院大学教授の山下裕二氏が〈猫を描いた近代日本画として最高の達成だと思う〉と展覧会図録で述べている作品。《紅梅・白梅》は、妙子館長が祖父・種二氏のひざに乗せられて見ていた作品だという。上村松園・松篁親子は、種二が懇意にしていた画家。特に松園の作品は、妙子館長の祖母、つまり種二氏の夫人が特に愛好していたという。

高価な群青の絵具をふんだんに使った川端龍子の《鳴門》、素描的な描写を意図的に試みたといわれる土田麦僊の《大原女》などの大作、柴田是真の漆絵30図を収めた画帖――収集作品のヴァラエティーは実に豊かで、種二氏の鑑賞眼の深さ、広さを物語る。

種二氏は、美術品収集を始めたころ、偽物の「酒井抱一の掛軸」を買ってしまったことがあったそうだ。そのときに「信用を第一とする商人が贋物を飾っていては、商売の信用にもかかわる」と思い、以降、各種展覧会に足を運んで目を養うとともに、多くの画商を通じて画家たちと交流し、直接作品を依頼するなどの関係になったという。前述した大観は、一時期、熱海の種二氏の別荘に滞在していたし、松園親子が京都から東京に来た際には、宿泊や食事などのアテンドをしていた。小林古径も交流のあった作家のひとり。道成寺伝説をもとにした《清姫》は発表当時から評価が高かった連作だが、《心神》と同様、「美術館を作るのであれば」ということで購入を許されたのだという。

山口蓬春の《新宮殿杉戸楓４分の１下絵》。皇居正殿松の間、東廊下の杉戸絵を手掛けた蓬春に、種二氏は同種画題の作品を依頼したが、病のため制作が進まず、1970年10月の同館「日本の四季」展に、この下絵が出品されたのだという。早世した速水御舟に種二氏は直接的な交流がなかったそうだが、その作品を深く尊敬しており、それが1976年の「安宅コレクション」の一括購入へとつながった。《昆虫二題》は1925年に描かれた重要文化財《炎舞》の後に描かれた同種感覚の作品で、光と闇、静と動のコントラストが印象的。

山種美術館は、1971～1997年には隔年で「山種美術館賞」を実施。2016（平成28）年からは公募展「Seed 山種美術館 日本画アワード」を定期的に開催。若手作家の発掘・育成にも努めている。それらの成果を描き下ろし作品とともに展示する「Ⅱ」は、日本画の現在地、あるいは将来への展望を示すものといえるだろう。逆に言えば、今回の「Ⅰ」は近代日本画の歩み、その果実を提示したものである。まずこの「Ⅰ」を鑑賞しておくことが、「Ⅱ」の鑑賞へとつながる。そういう意味でも、じっくり見ておくべき展覧会ではないか、とも思ったりするのである。（田中 聡）

"拉斐尔前派深知：一切都在于头发。在那些以鲜明写实著称的19世纪英国艺术家所绘的众多溺水女性图像中（奥菲莉亚是常见的题材），我们的目光总被头发吸引：那长长的、飘散的秀发，平直而松散，发丝垂落在女人的肩头，或漂浮在水中，四散开来。这些画作是性被动与顺从的幻象；为爱而自溺的美丽女子，是19世纪欧洲人的一种恋物式执念——不仅是诗人和画家，还有世纪之交许多购买“塞纳河无名女尸”死亡面具的中产阶级人士，那是一位据称从巴黎的河中打捞上来的无名女子。溺水的女性使观者得以在情感上否认性侵犯；她是欧洲父权制的原型图像之一，并普遍萦绕在我们对女性自杀与女性死亡驱力的再现之中。", "米拉格罗斯·穆门塔勒克制的剧情片《水流》与玛莎·席林斯基残酷的代际记忆之作《坠落之声》——两部影片均在第63届纽约电影节放映——以一种令人警醒的字面主义，复活了自溺女性的形象。在《坠落之声》中，故事在德国东北部一座庄园里四个世代的家庭之间流转——一个在第一次世界大战前，一个在纳粹时期，一个在1970年代，一个在当代——女孩和女人们跌入、潜入、闷闷不乐地跋涉进鳗鱼出没的易北河，阳光穿透水面照亮她们的身体。但她们拒绝溺水，转而选择某种自残与消失的形式，不容任何情色幻想。当我们确实看到女性尸体时，她们是令人不适的：一根针穿过祖母的眼睑；一个选择死亡而非被强奸的姐妹被支在长凳上，供人拍下一张阴森的家庭照片。", "对拉斐尔前派奥菲莉亚的指涉在《水流》中更为明确。穆门塔勒的影片以流畅的优雅、甚至光泽感展开，这掩盖了它的政治冲击力。伊莎贝尔·艾梅·冈萨雷斯·索拉有着一头长而美丽的头发，当她的角色莉娜停止洗头时，看到它变得油腻、打结，像发胶固定成头盔一般，缠成一团，令人一震。莉娜那场模棱两可的自杀尝试，以芭蕾般的冷峻优雅拍摄——在日内瓦接受一项专业奖项后，她走过城市，穿过一座桥，突然翻过栏杆，跳入河中——发生在影片最初的几分钟里。其余部分聚焦于她回到丈夫和年幼女儿身边、回到她们在布宜诺斯艾利斯的高档住宅之后发生的事，在那里她完全停止淋浴，无法忍受流水的感觉，甚至无法忍受流水的声音。", 世纪另一幅描绘被娇养的女人几乎溺水的画面：亨利克·易卜生剧作《玩偶之家》中的那一幕，其中包含这位剧作家对当时已成陈词滥调的女性投水自尽情节的尖锐批判。在《玩偶之家》中，主人公娜拉幻想以溺水自尽作为对丈夫的爱的牺牲；当他证明自己完全不值得时，她转而决定离开他和孩子们，开始新生活。与娜拉不同，莉娜在离开的路上改变了主意，回到尖叫的孩子身边；母女俩最后的画面在情感上如同莉娜的濒死一样暧昧不明，但其中有一种脆弱的平静。《坠落之声》的结尾却没有这样的平静，当代那户人家的小女儿突然从谷仓的阁楼上跳下。如果说 Schilinski 影片的结尾指向无意识创伤在代际间的爆发，那么 Mumenthaler 的影片所唤起的则是某种不那么惊心动魄、却同样本质的东西：有时候，不死就是最好的报复。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
The Pre-Raphaelites knew: it’s all about the hair. In the many images of drowned women (Ophelia was a regular subject) painted by the 19th-century British artists known for their vivid realism, it’s the hair our eyes are drawn to: the long, flowing locks, lank and loose, with tendrils tumbling over the woman’s shoulders or floating, splayed out, in the water. These paintings are visions of sexual passivity and submission; the beautiful woman who drowns herself for love was a fetishistic fixation of 19th-century Europeans—not just poets and painters, but also the many middle-class people around the turn of the century who bought death masks of “L’Inconnu de la Seine,” an anonymous woman whose body was supposedly pulled from the Paris river. The drowned woman enables the spectator’s sentimental disavowal of sexual aggression; she is one of the ur-images of European patriarchy, and she haunts our representations of women’s suicides and the feminine death drive more generally.

Milagros Mumenthaler’s restrained drama The Currents and Mascha Schilinski’s brutal intergenerational memory piece Sound of Falling —both of which screened at the 63rd NYFF—revive the image of the self-drowned woman with a bracing literalism. In Sound of Falling , which moves among four generations of families—one pre–World War I, one during the Nazi era, one in the 1970s, and one contemporary—on an estate in northeast Germany, girls and women fall, dive, and trudge sullenly into the eel-infested Elbe river, their bodies illuminated by the sun rays piercing the water’s surface. But they refuse to drown, choosing instead forms of self-harm and disappearance that disallow any fantasy of eroticism. When we do see female corpses, they are nasty: a needle runs through a grandmother’s eyelids; a sister who has chosen death over rape is propped up on a bench for a macabre family photo.

The camerawork of Sound of Falling has a blurry, gauzy remove, but bursts of unplaceable sound underscore moments of emotional intensity with expressionistic force. The first historical scenes, of a farming family and their servants, evoke early uses of photography for spiritualism and the occult, and the ghostly atmosphere deepens as Schilinski and DP Fabian Gamper’s camera zeroes in on bodily wounds and violence—brothers with amputated legs, maids sterilized for repeated rape, eels with their bared teeth sunk into human flesh. As these examples suggest, Schilinski and her collaborators are interested most of all in phallic weaponry, which makes it something of a shock when, in the contemporary scene of a bohemian family renovating the house, a woman gently tugs her husband’s penis out of his jeans. In these sections set in the more recent past, focused on adolescent girls and their loving but uncomprehending mothers, the film loses some steam without the active threat of the almost archaic violence of the first two generations, but continues to coalesce into resonant imagery—a mother trapped in a car parked between two trees; girls pulled on a mattress across a floor, as if on a raft.

Reference to the Pre-Raphaelite Ophelia is more pointed in The Currents . Mumenthaler’s film unfolds with a smooth elegance, even glossiness, that belies its political punch. Isabel Aimé González Sola has long and beautiful hair, and when her character, Lina, stops washing it, it’s a jolt to see it become greasy and matted, gelled into a helmet and tangled in knots. Lina’s ambiguous suicide attempt, shot with the cold grace of a ballet—after accepting a professional award in Geneva, she walks through the city, crosses a bridge, climbs suddenly over the railing, and jumps into the river—occurs in the first few minutes of the film . The rest focuses on what happens after she returns to her husband and young daughter and their upscale home in Buenos Aires, where she stops showering completely, incapable of tolerating the feeling or even the sound of running water.

The shock when Lina pulls her dirty hair off her neck to reveal a red rash on her scalp is eclipsed only by the scene that follows it: after weeks (or longer) of being unable to bathe, Lina finds herself in the back room of a hair salon, where she is fitted with a face mask and put under general anesthesia so that the beautician—whom she knows from her past—can wash her body and hair. It took me a minute to realize that there’s novocaine in the salon because customers go there for medicalized beauty procedures, commonplace among contemporary bourgeois women. It’s a scene that shifts The Currents decisively from a character study about a privileged woman’s inexplicable alienation toward a consideration of class-stratified women’s labor that echoes in the film ’s penultimate sequence, when Lina goes to visit her mother in a working-class suburb.

The final scenes of Mumenthaler’s film put me in mind of another 19th-century representation of a cossetted woman’s almost-drowning: the one in Henrik Ibsen’s play A Doll House , which includes the playwright’s scathing critique of the by-then cliché of a woman’s suicide by water. In A Doll House , protagonist Nora fantasizes about drowning herself as a sacrifice of love to her husband; when he proves himself utterly unworthy, she decides instead to start a new life without him and their children. Lina, unlike Nora, changes her mind on her way out, returning to her screaming child; the final images of mother and daughter are as emotionally ambiguous as Lina’s near-death, but there’s a fragile peace in them. There’s no such calmness at the end of Sound of Falling , as the younger daughter of the contemporary family jumps suddenly from the loft of a barn. If the end of Schilinski’s film points to the eruption of unconscious trauma through generations, Mumenthaler’s evokes something less spectacular but no less essential: sometimes not dying is the best revenge.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Actress Alice Eve has inked with Verve and lined up a new project: a grief-themed indie called The Long Run that’s slated for production this fall.

In The Long Run , Eve plays Claire Stanton, a woman shattered by the loss of her Marine husband who rediscovers life thanks to the unruly rescue dog he left behind — an unlikely companion who pulls her, mile by mile, toward the marathon they once promised to run together and a deeper connection with her young son.

Harold Cronk ( Unbroken: Path to Redemption ) is directing from a screenplay by Liz Larsen and Brando Colonna. Leeni Marshall is producing for Rare Films.

On the film side, Eve’s credits include J.J. Abrams’ Star Trek Into Darkness , Men in Black 3 , action thriller Cold Comes The Night opposite Bryan Cranston, and romantic comedy She’s Out of My League opposite Jay Baruchel. Her television credits include Netflix’s Black Mirror , Marvel’s Iron Fist and the historical drama Belgravia from Julian Fellowes.

Watch on Deadline

Eve continues to be represented by Artist International Group, with whom she signed in August, as well as ARG in the UK, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

Round one…fight!

“Street Fighter” is back on the big screen for a new take on the popular fighting game video series that started back in arcades in the 1980s and is still popular today.

Paramount and Legendary’s live-action movie takes place in the ’90s and follows a worldwide fighting tournament that brings together challengers from around the world. The roster includes Ken Masters (Noah Centineo) and his childhood friend and training partner Ryu (Andrew Koji), who have appeared in every “Street Fighter” video game. There’s a colorful cast of fellow characters like Chun-Li (Callina Liang), M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), Cammy (Mel Jarnson), Vega (Orville Peck) and more. The cast also has several real-life martial arts fighters, WWE stars and wrestlers, like Roman Reigns as Akuma, Cody Rhodes as Guile and Oliver Richters as Zangief.

Kitao Sakurai, who’s helmed episodes of “Beef,” “Dave” and the “Eric Andre Show,” directs the movie, which previously had Danny and Michael Philippou (“Talk to Me,” “Bring Her Back) attached. It’s actually the third “Street Fighter” movie, following 1994’s self-titled film and the 2009 release “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li.” The 1994 “Street Fighter” had a cast with Jean-Claude Van Damme as Guile, Ming-Na Wen as Chun-Li, Damian Chapa as Ken, Byron Mann as Ryu and Kylie Minogue as Cammy. “The Legend of Chun-Li” was a notorious flop and included Kristin Kreuk as Chun-Li, Neal McDonough as M. Bison, Michael Clarke Duncan as Balrog and Black Eyed Peas singer Taboo as Vega.

See the full cast of the new “Street Fighter” movie and how they compare to their video game counterparts below.

Ken (Noah Centineo) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Alongside Ryu, Ken has appeared in every single main “Street Fighter” video game. In the movie, he’s a loudmouth, washed-up celebrity who’s trying to claw his back way to fighting stardom after his childhood friend and training partner Ryu has become the world champion. Ken is known for his fireball hadoken fireball move, his Dragon Punch flying uppercut (aka the shoryuken) and his tornado kick attack. Noah Centineo plays Ken after starring in movies like “To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before,” “Black Adam” and “Warfare.”

Ryu (Andrew Koji) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Like Ken, Ryu is the only other character who’s been on every “Street Fighter” roster. He’s normally wearing his classic white gi, red headband and red gloves, and he has similar hadoken and shoryuken moves like Ken. They’re among the most popular characters in fighting games and have crossed over into other titles like “Super Smash Bros.,” “Marvel vs. Capcom” and more. Ryu is played by Andrew Koji, an actor and martial artist who played Storm Shadow in “Snake Eyes” and starred in “Bullet Train” and “Warrior.”

Chun-Li (Callina Liang) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Chun-Li first appeared in “Street Fighter 2” and was one of the first female characters in any fighting game. She’s known for her kick attacks (and impressively large thighs) and her iconic blue costume. Chun-Li seeks out revenge against M. Bison after he murdered her father. Callina Liang bulked up and trained for the movie after appearing in “Presence” and “Bad Genius.”

Cammy (Mel Jarnson) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Cammy works for the evil M. Bison as one of his agents. She was introduced in “Street Fighter 2: The New Warriors” and was the second female character added to the series after Chun-Li. Her costume has become popular among fans for her green or blue leotard, military beret and long braided pigtails. She’s played by Mel Jarnson, who also appeared in the “Mortal Kombat” movie as Nitara.

M. Bison (David Dastmalchian) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection M. Bison is a villain and often the final boss in the “Street Fighter” games. He’s a megalomaniac dictator who rules over the Shadaloo criminal syndicate, and characters like Cammy, Vega and Juli report to him. He grows stronger from harvesting Psycho Power, and he’s often wearing a red military uniform. David Dastmalchian stars as the villain after playing equally odd characters in “The Suicide Squad,” “Dune” and “One Piece.”

Dan Hibiki (Andrew Schulz) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Dan Hibiki is a comically weak fighter who also trained under Gouken alongside Ryu and Ken. With his pink gi, Dan later becomes a more respected and well-rounded fighter, but his moves are animated to be comedic in the video games. He’s played by comedian Andrew Schulz, who’s started appearing in more movies after growing to fame with his stand-up.

Akuma (Roman Reigns) Akuma is one of the most powerful villains in “Street Fighter” and the younger brother of Gouten, mentor to Ryu and Ken. He’s often the final boss in many of the games and uses dark energy to power his hadokens. WWE star Roman Reigns plays Akuma in the movie.

Guile (Cody Rhodes) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Guile is a U.S. Air force pilot seeking revenge against M. Bison. He’s dressed in military fatigues and has an American flag tattoo, but he’s best known for his odd, flat-top blond haircut. He’s played by WWE star Cody Rhodes in his largest film role to date.

Zangief (Olivier Richters) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Zangief is a massive Soviet wrestler known for his grappling moves, red shorts, X-shaped scars and hairy chest. He’s played by bodybuilder Olivier Richters, who stands at 7’2” and has acted in “Reacher,” “Black Widow,” “Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny” and fellow video game movie “Borderlands.”

Vega (Orville Peck) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Vega is a Spanish fighter who sports a mask and razor-sharp claws in all of his appearances. He uses a mix of Japanese ninjutsu and Spanish bullfighting in his combat. He’s played by country singer Orville Peck, who’s making his film debut and is also almost always seen wearing a mask in his performances.

Blanka (Jason Momoa) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Blanka is a green-skinned, orange-haired monster who can generate electricity and launch himself as a super-fast ball, his signature move. He’s an animalistic fighter who’s controlled by M. Bison, and Jason Momoa plays the character after appearing in films like “Aquaman,” “Dune,” “Supergirl” and “Minecraft.”

Balrog (50 Cent) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Balrog is a boxer who enters the fighting tournament and is played by rapper, actor and business mogul Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson. He wears his blue boxing outfit, but is better known for his unique hairstyle that paid homage to boxer Mike Tyson.

Dhalsim (Vidyut Jammwal) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Dhalsim is a stretchy, Indian yogi and fighter who can contort his limbs. He’s played by Vidyut Jammwal, an Indian actor and martial artist making his American feature film debut.

Gouken (Don Lee) Image Credit: a Gouken is the mentor to Ryu and Ken who’s later murdered by his evil brother Akuma. He’s played by Don Lee, who’s starred in movies like “Train to Busan,” “Eternals” and many more and has a background in martial arts.

E. Honda (Hirooki Goto) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection E. Honda is a sumo fighter played by Hirooki Goto, an actor and professional wrestler making his American feature film debut.

Juli (Rayna Vallandingham) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Juli is one of M. Bison’s minions who’s played by actress and martial artist Rayna Vallandingham (“Cobra Kai,” “Citadel”).

Don Sauvage (Eric Andre) Don Sauvage is an announcer and non-playable character introduced more recently in “Street Fighter 5.” He’s played by comedian Eric Andre.

Joe (Alexander Volkanovski) Joe is a non-playable background character who appeared in the first “Street Fighter” game. He’s played by Alexander Volkanovski, an MMA fighter and two-time UFC champion.

article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2024 Sundance coverage under the title Little Death. The film arrives on MUBI on October 23.

Maybe you’re vexed by the official description for Junk , the debut feature from music-video director Jack Begert. Maybe you want to know more than, “A middle-aged filmmaker on the verge of a breakthrough. Two kids in search of a lost backpack. A small dog a long way from home.” Maybe you’re itching to search for a more detailed plot description.

Take my word for it: don’t.

The worst thing about Junk , which Begert co-wrote with Dani Goffstein, is that the best things about it are all spoilers. Please excuse some vagueness in the interest of your best possible moviegoing experience.

David Schwimmer, fully leaning into the self-pitying act he honed as Ross Geller, plays Martin, the middle-aged filmmaker. Martin’s life is, as he tells his therapist, “meaningless.” A long-suffering TV writer, Martin’s finally got an autobiographical script in the works, but wokeism threatens his masterpiece. He abhors his fiancée, Jess (Jena Malone), who commits such unforgivable acts as blending things in their blender and expecting him to listen when he talks. A vast cocktail of psychiatric meds hasn’t cured his misery, but it’s not all bad––he dreams nightly about a sexy woman in a barn. The kids are Karla (Talia Ryder) and AJ (Dominic Fike), two druggies caught up in the absurd underbelly of L.A. The small dog unites these disparate storylines.

Junk is probably one of the most surprising films you’ll see this year. Begert and Goffstein’s script is wonderfully unique, while the former ably switches from eye-popping visuals to patient observation. Martin’s world is vibrant and overloaded, chock-full of violent imagery and flashes of unsettling AI art. Editor Jake Torchin really earns his stripes in these scenes, cutting between frames so rapidly that the end result resembles a stop-motion panic attack. He and Begert have created a perfect representation of what it looks like inside the brain of a person with incurable neuroses. Karla and AJ’s exploits are depicted with more subtlety but no less artfully, and Ryder and Fike give fantastic performances. Newcomer Sante Bentivoglio makes a meal of his first-ever feature role as he butts heads with the always-great Karl Glusman ( Watcher ).

This film is mostly about human fragility and drugs; no surprise Darren Aronofsky produced it. Like an unsympathetic Nina Sayers, Martin is losing himself in obsession––with the sexy barn lady, his movie, his waning relevance in pop culture. Karla, AJ, and the people who love them are singing their own Requiem for a Dream . But Begert sets himself apart from Aronofsky’s dour oeuvre with delicacy and humor. Martin is the unwitting protagonist of a satire about cancel culture and the paranoia of the privileged, demonstrating how the derision of hypocrites––in this case, moviemakers who measure diversity by quantity, not quality––can make a shitty guy even shittier. Karla and AJ are lovable for all their youthful stupidity, especially because they really care about each other as friends.

As Junk zig-zags like a sidewinder in the desert, Begert strikes a neat balance between esoteric inscrutability and blunt messaging. It’s nice to see a first-time director unafraid to let his viewers have their own experiences and come to their own conclusions. Here’s one: the bravest thing about Junk isn’t its risks––it’s the filmmakers’ choice to forgo nihilism for hope.

Junk premiered at the 2024 Sundance Film Festival.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 这是 Gessica Généus 继《Freda》（2021）之后的第二部长片，这部炽烈的海地寓言将宗教的无处不在与卖淫所代表的越界相对峙。也再次印证了这位女导演多面的才华。

article_text:
Après le remarqué Freda, qui dépeignait le quotidien d’une famille habitant un quartier populaire de Port-au-Prince, Gessica Généus poursuit sa peinture flamboyante d’Haïti en déplaçant ici son regard vers Jacmel, ville maritime du sud-est du pays fortement marquée par la présence de la religion.

Vivant du travail du sexe dans une maison close située en face d’un temple protestant, Marie Madeleine (jouée par la cinéaste elle-même) se prend d’affection pour Joseph (Béonard Monteau), un jeune évangéliste idéaliste mais écrasé par la figure de son père (Édouard Baptiste), pasteur colérique qui exprime publiquement sa haine contre les prostituées locales.

À travers les relations mouvementées animant ce trio de personnages, Gessica Généus exhibe toutes les forces contraires qui agitent la société haïtienne, entre foi persistante, misère sociale, désirs amoureux, culture vaudoue, peurs morales ou difficulté à se créer un espace d’intimité. Au moyen d’un étalonnage aux couleurs éclatantes et d’une théâtralité enivrante, la mise en scène illustre à merveille la fièvre qui s’empare des esprits. Et permet d’entrevoir la beauté fragile d’un sentiment d’émancipation qui peut résister furtivement à la brutalité.

article_text:
Interview

Layli Long Soldier’s Poetic Lifeblood

I spoke to the poet, who is my longtime friend and colleague, about her new book, the threads connecting poetry and visual art, and how Lakota philosophy suffuses her work.

Reading Layli Long Soldier’s newest publication, We (Graywolf Press, 2026), is a visual experience. She leads us across the page through poetry and storytelling, but her work is far more than ideas, statements, and wordplay. Even when just text on the page, it is both literature and visual art. Through this bridge, it creates deep connections to our innermost experiences — at times validating our own humanity, or providing a window into another’s. Fittingly, the title has two meanings: the English “we” and the Lakota “wé,” meaning “blood,” a shared lineage and life source.

Layli and I first met while we were both attending the Institute of American Indian Arts in Santa Fe, New Mexico. As fellow Lakota in the Southwest, art students, and mothers, we bonded quickly. Our now-grown children played together when they were toddlers. We have continued to support and cheer one another on throughout the past 20 years as friends and colleagues. I am thrilled to have been able to spend dedicated time with her new book. Readers will recognize the strength and unique literary style Layli demonstrated in her 2017 poetry collection Whereas , while experiencing the excitement and joy of new terrain offered in this moving body of exploratory and expansive work.

We (Wé) is life-affirming, motivating, a call to action, an instigator of deep critical thinking; it binds together our history and our present. It is advocacy and truth-telling, education, and inquiry, all through a lens of lived experience, compassion, and love. It is an artistic expression led by Lakota values and philosophy and, through this, connects to humanity at large. Our conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Dyani White Hawk: You utilize text placement, formatting, omission, symbols, color, rhythm, pauses, reader choices, and instructional language to paint rich visuals in each section of this book. There are essays and short stories, photographs, and visual art scattered throughout. You are a poet, and you are an artist. Can you please speak to the process of how you find form for a work? Do you see the shape in advance? The color? Do the words come first, and reveal their shape?

Layli Long Soldier: First of all, thank you so much, Dyani, for such a beautiful introduction to my work. And I, too, identify so deeply with your work. I think a lot about process. And in your work, I recognize the time, meticulous detail, the math, the planning, the patience, and likewise, the sensitivity to color, shape, and underlying meaning and philosophy that you put into your pieces.

Some of the forms for my poems are really demanding. They require tight use of space, down to the centimeter, at times, e.g., the poems in A Line Through Grief or Obligations . Even when the form requires every last bit of patience, believe it or not, my friends and relatives who do beadwork or detailed sculptural pieces inspire me. I think to myself, if they can sit and patiently pick up one bead at a time with a needle, then I can practice that kind of attention as well! So I keep going.

Sometimes the form in my poems does come first. I’ll wake up in the morning and I can see a shape. It feels almost as if a shape is waving hello, inviting me. So I go to my laptop with a general idea of what I want the poem to look like. And this, then, becomes the first constraint. I begin building the poem from there.

But sometimes, it’s the language that comes first. Perhaps I’m thinking about an experience, a memory, or a person, and this is where I begin. I enter the quiet mental excavation for words to translate a feeling or idea onto the page. Once the language feels right, I’ll begin the next stage of trial and error to find the right form. There have been some poems that take months or years to complete because of this process. Yet it’s so rewarding once I do find the right form, because suddenly the poem gets traction and starts to move. I can feel it in my body, it’s as if the poem says, “Thank you!”

DWH: I also really appreciate the kind, gentle, strong yet nurturing way you very intentionally lead readers through a work with commands, reminders, and encouragement. You work to ensure that they remember to hear, see, and feel what is being offered. Do you feel this is related to who you are as a Lakota artist? As a woman? As an Indigenous artist?

LLS: I’m not really sure why I do this in my writing, except it is my nature. In some ways, I consider the reader a guest. Isn’t it funny that “stanza” means room? So you could say that as I invite guests into a poem, I am guiding them through the rooms of a kind of home that I’ve built.

Also, over the years, I’ve developed an awareness that there are many ways — techniques or approaches — to help a reader feel comfortable enough to stay with me, even when I’m diving into difficult subject matter. Sometimes, I press hard. For example, in my essay “Through the Pupil of Instinct” [in We ], I share painful first-hand accounts from survivors of the Wounded Knee Massacre. Yet, the essay moves multi-directionally, shifting from Wounded Knee to my child’s day at school to a drive through Minneapolis with my poet friend, Heid Erdrich. These shifts allow the reader time and breath to endure the moments of intensity. I want to say what I need to say, I want to “go there” when it comes to harm, violence, or injustice, but I also want readers to be able to sustain the energy it takes to go there with me.

article_text:
Veteran Hollywood publicist Gene Schwam , who represented top talent including Elvis Presley , Blake Edwards, Julie Andrews, Barbara Eden and Lenny Bruce, died Friday in Los Angeles after a brief illness. He was 96.

Schwam co-founded Hanson & Schwam Public Relations with Adeline Hanson in 1955, establishing an independent publicity agency that would endure for decades.

Schwam was earning $35 a week working for publicist Stanley Cowan when he decided to strike out on his own. He joined forces with Hanson, a part-time disc jockey and publicist, to launch their firm. When it came time to decide whose name would come first, Schwam wanted his own name at the front. Hanson’s response settled the matter: “Ladies first.”

Starting with Smith Bros. Fish Shanty restaurant as their first client, Hanson & Schwam grew into an enduring presence in entertainment publicity, with Schwam continuing as president and co-founder decades later.

Popular on Variety

Clients included Nancy Wilson and Lou Rawls, as well as the famous Coconut Grove nightclub, which helped the agency foster relationships with numerous entertainers.

His colorful representation (and intentional misreputation) of Presley in 1957 was covered in Variety at the time of the release of Baz Luhrmann’s “Elvis” in 2022. Schwam’s longtime relationship with Edwards extended beyond the professional. He was a friend as well as a publicist to the legendary director of such classics as “Breakfast at Tiffany’s,” “10,” and“Victor/Victoria.”

Edwards’ character of the neurotic publicist in his film “S.O.B.” was based on Schwam. That friendship reflected something fundamental about Schwam’s approach: he was known for his passionate engagement and resourceful guidance of his clients’ careers.

Vernon Scott, the longtime United Press International entertainment correspondent, called him “The best idea man in Hollywood,” a description that captured the inventive thinking at the center of Schwam’s work.

Later in life, Schwam created Humanity 101, an initiative of Arizona State University’s Project Humanities, promoting the values of compassion, empathy, forgiveness, integrity, kindness, respect and self-reflection.

He is survived by his wife, Myrna; daughter Stephanie Schwam (Instagram contact @youreprettyandnice); stepchildren Adam, Greg and Linda London; and five grandchildren.

article_text:
Among Florida Governor Ron DeSantis ’s favorite activities since he took office is pooh-poohing climate change initiatives while, almost surreptitiously, working to conserve swathes of the state he represents. Now, a group of environmental activists has found a way to make him sweat.

A life-size statue of the Republican governor was unveiled in Tallahassee last week, only to begin melting in the Florida sunshine. As DeSantis’s silver-colored face slowly slipped away, a dastardly-looking skull appeared underneath. According to The Guardian , it was all part of the plan.

The installation, titled DENIAL , was made from gallium, a metal that melts at just 85.6 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature that Florida residents are more than familiar with.

The work was organized by environmental group 350 Action, advertising agency Uncommon, and too-cleverly named production company M ss ng P eces. Its message was fairly simple: Climate change is real, whether the governor wants to acknowledge it or not.

DeSantis, whose second and final term ends in January, has been a vocal opponent of climate policies he considers excessive. In 2024, he signed legislation that removed references to climate change and greenhouse gas emissions from Florida law and limited the ability of local governments to pursue certain environmental policies.

“We’re restoring sanity in our approach to energy and rejecting the agenda of the radical green zealots,” DeSantis wrote on X at the time.

Florida, of course, has plenty of reasons to worry about rising temperatures. The state faces growing risks from sea-level rise and ferocious hurricanes. Then of course there’s soaring insurance costs, which have become a serious problem for homeowners.

The activists behind DENIAL also had an eye on November’s elections. With DeSantis leaving office, they hope the disappearing sculpture will encourage voters to consider where candidates stand on climate policy.

“The climate crisis is one of the top issues facing our planet today,” Candice Fortin, campaign manager at 350 Action, told The Guardian . She argued that candidates who reject climate action should face the consequences at the ballot box. The installation, it seems, was as much a political advertisement as a work of public art, designed to deliver its message before the whole thing melts away.

第４週 「岩国と、共に」

大正4年、珠（石橋静河）が教員を辞めさせられてから、葉野家の収入はリョウ（国仲涼子）が工場で働く稼ぎだけだった。月日が経っても教師が不らちな 逢引 をした、という噂は消えなかったため、珠の新しい仕事もなかなか見つからない。そこでリョウが本家の葉野酒造に頼み込み、珠がそこで働くことに。そんな時、かつて嫁入りした花婿の弟・木村保（金子大地）と偶然出会い…。

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“圣像：幻想的图像”是与埃皮纳勒图像博物馆多年合作项目的一部分，由克里斯黛尔·罗谢特（Christelle Rochette）担任策展指导。她发起了一项基于该馆馆藏及当代新增作品、对圣像图像地位的反思。2024年，埃皮纳勒的展览（2月24日 – 9月22日）探讨了神话与传说、非凡的命运、磁性的光环以及大众的崇拜，阐明了图像的制造与圣像的幻想。对于穆然而言，精选的作品体量经过调整与重构，透过摄影工业及其在人类将自我投射到他人躯体中的需求——不仅仅是随便哪个人，而是一个近乎神圣、剥离了所有歧义或不完美、最重要的是切断了与世界联系的存在——这一棱镜得到了重新诠释。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "导言", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当代世界充斥着图像。其中，一些图像获得了特殊的力量，甚至升格为圣像的地位。该词源自希腊语 eikôn（意为“图像”），最初指的是东正教传统的圣事再现。它逐渐延伸到世俗领域，用来描述那些其图像似乎超越了自身存在的形象。这种转变既取决于图像，也取决于观看它的人。圣像仅通过赋予其象征价值、沉思它、复制它并由此助长其力量的崇拜者、信徒或观看者群体而存在。它成为集体信仰的场所，介于迷恋、崇拜和投射之间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，在圣经传统中，圣像与偶像不同。偶像声称将神性封闭在可见的形式之内。相比之下，圣像的价值仅在于它所揭示的不可见之物——一个想象中的彼岸。人们崇拜它不是为了它本身，而是作为超越它的存在的标志。随着摄影的出现，紧接着是电影和大众传媒，这种与图像的关系发生了深刻的转变。机械复制使能够获得圣像地位的人物成倍增加，从圣徒到英雄，从烈士到重生的圣像。本次展览探讨了图像与信仰之间、被呈现者与那些通过自己的目光、崇拜或虔诚来帮助赋予他们超越现实的自主存在者之间的这种张力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次展览分为12个章节，每个章节围绕一个标志性人物展开：", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "基督：真正的圣像", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "英雄游击队员", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "玛丽莲、诺玛·简、泽尔达·宗克", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "上帝之手，或圣迭戈的一生", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "陵墓", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "帕德雷·皮奥的附伤", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "披头士狂热", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "约翰尼化名", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "BB：新夏娃", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "戴安娜与第十三根柱子", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "6月18日：言即行", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "弗里达·卡洛，或墨西哥痛苦主义", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "圣像 基督：真正的圣像 基督的面容无疑是世界上最广为人知的图像，尽管没有任何文本描述过他的外貌。福音书对此保持沉默，最早的表象出现在他逝世两个世纪之后。因此，基督教的历史在某种程度上也是一个逐渐构建起一个不容置疑的人物形象的历史。从拜占庭的万王之王到圣容，从曼迪利昂圣容到受难的基督，再到后来的好牧人，每个时代都塑造了一个反映自身精神与政治期许的图像。在19世纪，基督变成了一个更亲近、更能抚慰人心的形象。随着华纳·萨尔曼（Warner Sallman）作品的问世，并自1940年代起广泛传播，西方关于浅色眼睛基督的形象最终确立为世界上被复制最多的宗教圣像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "英雄游击队员", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅拍摄于1960年“拉库布雷号”爆炸遇难者纪念活动上的照片，即科达（Korda）的《英雄游击队员》，在切·格瓦拉于1967年逝世后，成为了20世纪最具象征意义的图像之一以及真正的邪典圣像。他正面而威严的面孔超越了单纯的政治肖像，融入了殉难的基督般的圣像学中。他在玻利维亚的逝世以及后来对其遗体公开展示的照片，让人想起受难记（Passion）中的场景。被打败的游击队员变成了一个注定要获得象征性复活的牺牲形象。肖像的裁剪凸显了目光和贝雷帽上的五角星，产生了一种类似显圣（transfiguration）的效果。就像宗教圣像一样，这幅图像脱离了这个人，成为了反叛和救赎的普遍标志。1968年后广为流传，它获得了现代曼迪利昂圣容的力量，随后在商业复制中逐渐失去了其政治色彩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "玛丽莲、诺玛·简、泽尔达·宗克", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "玛丽莲·梦露体现了人类形态的圣像，一个诞生于自我完全暴露之中的泥人（Golem），其中诺玛·简为自己被塑造成普遍的欲望客体付出了代价。她的神话建立在悲剧之上，需要通过他人的目光来获得认同，她的一生被塑造成了一部摄影小说，介于情节剧与牺牲之间。为了逃离自己的形象，玛丽莲在玛丽莲和诺玛·简之间摇摆不定，之后将自己发明为泽尔达·宗克。照片中显现的分裂自我让她饱受撕裂，每一个姿势都揭示了她内心的挣扎。她通过黑白摄影沙龙寻求对自身形象的控制，变成了一种无路可走的视觉精神分析。她在文字和治疗中暴露出的内疚和内心冲突，不可避免地导致了一个悲剧性的结局，从而注定她作为圣像的命运。在她逝世后，她真正的躯体变得多余了，因为圣像已经属于全世界。", article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Icons: Fantasised Images is part of a collaboration spanning several years with the Musée de l’Image in Épinal, under the direction of Christelle Rochette, who initiated a reflection on the status of iconic images drawing on its collections and contemporary additions. In 2024, the exhibition in Épinal (February 24 – September 22) explored myths and legends, extraordinary destinies, magnetic aura, and mass devotion, shedding light on the making of the image and the fantasy of the icon. For Mougins, the selected body of work has been adapted and reimagined through the prism of the photographic industry and its role in humanity’s need to project itself into the body of another – not just any other, but a quasi-divine being, stripped of all ambiguity or imperfection and, above all, cut off from the world."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Introduction"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The contemporary world is saturated with images. Among them, some acquire a particular force, even rising to the status of icon. Derived from the Greek eikôn (‘image’), the term originally designated the sacred representations of the Eastern Christian tradition. It gradually extended into the secular realm to describe figures whose image seems to transcend their very existence. This transformation depends as much on the image as on those who look at it. The icon exists only through a community of worshippers, believers, or viewers who grant it symbolic value, who contemplate it, reproduce it, and thereby contribute to its power. It becomes the site of a collective belief, somewhere between fascination, veneration, and projection."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the biblical tradition, however, the icon is distinct from the idol. The idol claims to enclose the divine within a visible form. The icon, by contrast, has value only in what it reveals of the invisible – of an imagined beyond. It is not worshipped for itself, but as the sign of a presence that transcends it. With the advent of photography, followed by cinema and mass media, this relationship to images was profoundly transformed. Mechanical reproduction multiplied the figures capable of attaining iconic status, from saint to hero, from martyr to icon reborn. The exhibition explores this tension between image and belief, between those who are represented and those who, through their gaze, admiration, or devotion, help give them an autonomous existence, beyond the real."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This exhibition is structured into twelve chapters, each centered around an iconic figure:"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Christ: The True Icon"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Guerrillero Heroico"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Marilyn, Norma Jean, Zelda Zonk"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The Hand of God, or the Life of Saint Diego"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Mausoleums"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The Transverberation of Padre Pio"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Beatlemania"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Alias Johnny"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "BB: The New Eve"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Diana and the Thirteenth Pillar"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "18 June: Speech as Act"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Frida Kahlo, or Mexican Dolorism"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Icons Christ: The True Icon The face of Christ is undoubtedly the most universally recognised image, even though no text describes his appearance. The Gospels remain silent, and the earliest representations appear only two centuries after his death. The history of Christianity is thus, in part, the story of the gradual construction of a figure who became unquestionable. From the Byzantine Pantocrator to the Holy Faces, from the Mandylion to the Suffering Christ, and later the Good Shepherd, each era shapes an image that reflects its own spiritual and political expectations. In the nineteenth century, Christ became a closer, more consoling figure. With the work of Warner Sallman, disseminated from the 1940s onward, the Western image of a Christ with light-coloured eyes became definitively established as the most widely reproduced religious icon in the world."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guerrillero Heroico"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Taken in 1960 at a memorial for the victims of the La Coubre explosion, Korda’s Guerrillero Heroico became, following Che Guevara’s death in 1967, one of the most emblematic images of the twentieth century and a true cult icon. His face, frontal and hieratic, transcends the mere political portrait to join a Christ-like iconography of martyrdom. His death in Bolivia, and the later photographs of his body on display, recall scenes from the Passion. The defeated guerrilla becomes a sacrificial figure, destined for symbolic resurrection. The cropping of the portrait, isolating the gaze and the star on his beret, effects a kind of transfiguration. Like a religious icon, the image detaches itself from the man to become a universal sign of revolt and redemption. Circulated after 1968, it acquired the force of a modern Mandylion, before gradually losing its political charge amid commercial reproduction."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Marilyn, Norma Jean, Zelda Zonk"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Marilyn Monroe embodies the icon in human form, a Golem born of total exposure of the self, in which Norma Jean pays the price for her transfiguration into a universal object of desire. Her myth, built on tragedy, requires identification through the gaze of others, a life fashioned like a photo-novel, somewhere between melodrama and sacrifice. Attempting to escape her image, Marilyn oscillated between Marilyn and Norma Jean, before inventing herself as Zelda Zonk. Torn by a divided self visible in her photographs, each pose reveals her inner struggle. Her quest for control over her image, through black-and-white photo sessions, becomes a form of visual psychoanalysis, with no way out. Guilt and inner conflicts, exposed in her writings and therapy sessions, lead inexorably to a tragic end, sealing her fate as an icon. After her death, her real body becomes superfluous, for the icon already belongs to the whole world."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Hand of God, or the Life of Saint Diego"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Maradona built his myth through a succession of contradictory images, caught between absolute glory and an inevitable fall. The ‘Hand of God’ in 1986, Argentina’s triumph, and the scudetto he brought to Naples elevated him to the status of a popular icon. His face became a relic of working-class neighbourhoods, preserved like that of a secular saint. Yet images of his decline – drugs, excess, and physical frailty – did not destroy his cult. On the contrary, they deepened his identification with the people, who forgave the weaknesses of the man who had avenged and represented them. Maradona thus became a Christ-like figure, a sacrificial hero whose contradictions are the very foundation of his immortality."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mausoleums"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Since the Entombment of Christ, the sacred body has oscillated between disappearance and presence, caught in an eternal tension. The remains of Lenin, Atatürk, Eva Perón, and Padre Pio, preserved from decay through embalming, extend this refusal of finitude. Behind the glass of mausoleums, the body becomes an image, tangible proof of a promised survival in which death is reduced to a passage. These modern relics, objects of belief and pilgrimage, answer the need for visible signs that can bind the living, the dead, and eternity together. Eva Perón, mummified in her glass coffin, embodies the untouchable icon, offering the descamisados a tangible form of redemption. Her myth, born of her commitment, transforms her remains into a sacred relic, venerated by crowds seeking certainty. These embalmed bodies, symbols of the transcendence of contradictions, assuage societies’ anxiety in the face of the void. The political or religious icon weaves a sacred bond between past, present, and a radiant future, beyond time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Transverberation of Padre Pio"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The image of Padre Pio has become one of the defining figures of contemporary Catholic devotion. His transverberation in 1918, experienced during the Eucharist and accompanied by the appearance of the stigmata, drew him closer to the suffering Christ and established the image of the ‘second Christ’. From this mystical experience onwards, his body became the vehicle of a belief, while his image spread far beyond Italy. Despite reservations within the Church and rationalist criticism, San Giovanni Rotondo became an international pilgrimage site. His cult, supported by political authorities and associated with charitable works, blends the religious, the social, and the symbolic. Canonised in 2002, his body became an icon-relic, extending the power of a figure situated between the human and the sacred."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Beatlemania"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Between 1963 and 1966, Beatlemania turned the Beatles into a true mass icon, inspiring a fervour akin to religious worship. The screaming, fainting, and adoration of fans testified to a fascination that went far beyond their music. Their image, disseminated through the press, television, and merchandise, became a powerful object of consumption. Their worldwide success was amplified by the rise of mass media, huge concerts, and programmes such as The Ed Sullivan Show . In 1967, their performance of ‘All You Need Is Love’, broadcast worldwide via Our World , consecrated their status as global icons. The Beatles embodied the cultural and social aspirations of the 1960s while also provoking fierce controversy, particularly after John Lennon’s claim that the group had become ‘more popular than Jesus’. Exhausted by Beatlemania and by an image that had become uncontrollable, they abandoned touring by 1966."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alias Johnny"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The ‘Johnnys’ (Johnny Christ, Johnny Rock, etc.) are not simply copies of Johnny Hallyday, but worshippers seeking an impossible fusion with the icon, attempting to embody the sacred image through rigorous discipline: imitating his gestures, voice, and clothes, to the point of effacing themselves. Their imitation goes beyond simple admiration. It is a form of voluntary servitude, a profound belief that refuses the void and fills the fear of absence. By relinquishing their identities, the Johnnys find their reward in the gaze of others, becoming image-subjects – reflections of an icon in which reality and imagination merge. Their lives, a freely chosen sacrifice, become a form of ecstasy, perpetuating the idol’s image at the cost of their own existence. For them, imitation is a form of transcendence, a mystical quest in which appearance becomes essence. Their autonomy lies in this absolute fidelity, through which the ideal self is realised in the infinite repetition of the fixed image. Their fascination with identification anchors them in a reality where the copy becomes truer than life itself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "BB: The New Eve"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Brigitte Bardot asserted a new kind of femininity, freed from the moral conventions of the post-war era. Natural and sensual, she associated desire with the freedom to choose without guilt. Simone de Beauvoir described her as an ‘Eve before original sin’, while Marguerite Duras saw her as a figure of emancipation. Her apparent innocence, combined with provocation, upended representations of femininity. Until the end of the 1960s, BB was emblematic of a modernity in which women’s autonomy asserted itself through the body as much as through attitude."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Diana and the Thirteenth Pillar"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The tunnel beneath the Pont de l’Alma, on 31 August 1997, ceased to be the mere setting of an accident and became the founding site of the myth of Lady Diana, a symbolic entrance to Hades. This dark passage, a threshold to the afterlife, marks her descent into the underworld, leaving the profane world behind for a sacred realm. The absence of images of her agony, hidden away like a taboo, reinforces the mystery of a modern martyrdom bordering on sainthood, leaving room for a succession of signs and imaginary images. article_text:
Icons: Fantasised Images is part of a collaboration spanning several years with the Musée de l’Image in Épinal, under the direction of Christelle Rochette, who initiated a reflection on the status of iconic images drawing on its collections and contemporary additions. In 2024, the exhibition in Épinal (February 24 – September 22) explored myths and legends, extraordinary destinies, magnetic aura, and mass devotion, shedding light on the making of the image and the fantasy of the icon. For Mougins, the selected body of work has been adapted and reimagined through the prism of the photographic industry and its role in humanity’s need to project itself into the body of another – not just any other, but a quasi-divine being, stripped of all ambiguity or imperfection and, above all, cut off from the world.

Introduction

The contemporary world is saturated with images. Among them, some acquire a particular force, even rising to the status of icon. Derived from the Greek eikôn (‘image’), the term originally designated the sacred representations of the Eastern Christian tradition. It gradually extended into the secular realm to describe figures whose image seems to transcend their very existence. This transformation depends as much on the image as on those who look at it. The icon exists only through a community of worshippers, believers, or viewers who grant it symbolic value, who contemplate it, reproduce it, and thereby contribute to its power. It becomes the site of a collective belief, somewhere between fascination, veneration, and projection.

In the biblical tradition, however, the icon is distinct from the idol. The idol claims to enclose the divine within a visible form. The icon, by contrast, has value only in what it reveals of the invisible – of an imagined beyond. It is not worshipped for itself, but as the sign of a presence that transcends it. With the advent of photography, followed by cinema and mass media, this relationship to images was profoundly transformed. Mechanical reproduction multiplied the figures capable of attaining iconic status, from saint to hero, from martyr to icon reborn. The exhibition explores this tension between image and belief, between those who are represented and those who, through their gaze, admiration, or devotion, help give them an autonomous existence, beyond the real.

This exhibition is structured into twelve chapters, each centered around an iconic figure:

Christ: The True Icon

Guerrillero Heroico

Marilyn, Norma Jean, Zelda Zonk

The Hand of God, or the Life of Saint Diego

Mausoleums

The Transverberation of Padre Pio

Beatlemania

Alias Johnny

BB: The New Eve

Diana and the Thirteenth Pillar

18 June: Speech as Act

Frida Kahlo, or Mexican Dolorism

Icons Christ: The True Icon The face of Christ is undoubtedly the most universally recognised image, even though no text describes his appearance. The Gospels remain silent, and the earliest representations appear only two centuries after his death. The history of Christianity is thus, in part, the story of the gradual construction of a figure who became unquestionable. From the Byzantine Pantocrator to the Holy Faces, from the Mandylion to the Suffering Christ, and later the Good Shepherd, each era shapes an image that reflects its own spiritual and political expectations. In the nineteenth century, Christ became a closer, more consoling figure. With the work of Warner Sallman, disseminated from the 1940s onward, the Western image of a Christ with light-coloured eyes became definitively established as the most widely reproduced religious icon in the world.

Guerrillero Heroico

Taken in 1960 at a memorial for the victims of the La Coubre explosion, Korda’s Guerrillero Heroico became, following Che Guevara’s death in 1967, one of the most emblematic images of the twentieth century and a true cult icon. His face, frontal and hieratic, transcends the mere political portrait to join a Christ-like iconography of martyrdom. His death in Bolivia, and the later photographs of his body on display, recall scenes from the Passion. The defeated guerrilla becomes a sacrificial figure, destined for symbolic resurrection. The cropping of the portrait, isolating the gaze and the star on his beret, effects a kind of transfiguration. Like a religious icon, the image detaches itself from the man to become a universal sign of revolt and redemption. Circulated after 1968, it acquired the force of a modern Mandylion, before gradually losing its political charge amid commercial reproduction.

Marilyn, Norma Jean, Zelda Zonk

Marilyn Monroe embodies the icon in human form, a Golem born of total exposure of the self, in which Norma Jean pays the price for her transfiguration into a universal object of desire. Her myth, built on tragedy, requires identification through the gaze of others, a life fashioned like a photo-novel, somewhere between melodrama and sacrifice. Attempting to escape her image, Marilyn oscillated between Marilyn and Norma Jean, before inventing herself as Zelda Zonk. Torn by a divided self visible in her photographs, each pose reveals her inner struggle. Her quest for control over her image, through black-and-white photo sessions, becomes a form of visual psychoanalysis, with no way out. Guilt and inner conflicts, exposed in her writings and therapy sessions, lead inexorably to a tragic end, sealing her fate as an icon. After her death, her real body becomes superfluous, for the icon already belongs to the whole world.

The Hand of God, or the Life of Saint Diego

Maradona built his myth through a succession of contradictory images, caught between absolute glory and an inevitable fall. The ‘Hand of God’ in 1986, Argentina’s triumph, and the scudetto he brought to Naples elevated him to the status of a popular icon. His face became a relic of working-class neighbourhoods, preserved like that of a secular saint. Yet images of his decline – drugs, excess, and physical frailty – did not destroy his cult. On the contrary, they deepened his identification with the people, who forgave the weaknesses of the man who had avenged and represented them. Maradona thus became a Christ-like figure, a sacrificial hero whose contradictions are the very foundation of his immortality.

Mausoleums

Since the Entombment of Christ, the sacred body has oscillated between disappearance and presence, caught in an eternal tension. The remains of Lenin, Atatürk, Eva Perón, and Padre Pio, preserved from decay through embalming, extend this refusal of finitude. Behind the glass of mausoleums, the body becomes an image, tangible proof of a promised survival in which death is reduced to a passage. These modern relics, objects of belief and pilgrimage, answer the need for visible signs that can bind the living, the dead, and eternity together. Eva Perón, mummified in her glass coffin, embodies the untouchable icon, offering the descamisados a tangible form of redemption. Her myth, born of her commitment, transforms her remains into a sacred relic, venerated by crowds seeking certainty. These embalmed bodies, symbols of the transcendence of contradictions, assuage societies’ anxiety in the face of the void. The political or religious icon weaves a sacred bond between past, present, and a radiant future, beyond time.

The Transverberation of Padre Pio

The image of Padre Pio has become one of the defining figures of contemporary Catholic devotion. His transverberation in 1918, experienced during the Eucharist and accompanied by the appearance of the stigmata, drew him closer to the suffering Christ and established the image of the ‘second Christ’. From this mystical experience onwards, his body became the vehicle of a belief, while his image spread far beyond Italy. Despite reservations within the Church and rationalist criticism, San Giovanni Rotondo became an international pilgrimage site. His cult, supported by political authorities and associated with charitable works, blends the religious, the social, and the symbolic. Canonised in 2002, his body became an icon-relic, extending the power of a figure situated between the human and the sacred.

Beatlemania

Between 1963 and 1966, Beatlemania turned the Beatles into a true mass icon, inspiring a fervour akin to religious worship. The screaming, fainting, and adoration of fans testified to a fascination that went far beyond their music. Their image, disseminated through the press, television, and merchandise, became a powerful object of consumption. Their worldwide success was amplified by the rise of mass media, huge concerts, and programmes such as The Ed Sullivan Show . In 1967, their performance of ‘All You Need Is Love’, broadcast worldwide via Our World , consecrated their status as global icons. The Beatles embodied the cultural and social aspirations of the 1960s while also provoking fierce controversy, particularly after John Lennon’s claim that the group had become ‘more popular than Jesus’. Exhausted by Beatlemania and by an image that had become uncontrollable, they abandoned touring by 1966.

Alias Johnny

The ‘Johnnys’ (Johnny Christ, Johnny Rock, etc.) are not simply copies of Johnny Hallyday, but worshippers seeking an impossible fusion with the icon, attempting to embody the sacred image through rigorous discipline: imitating his gestures, voice, and clothes, to the point of effacing themselves. Their imitation goes beyond simple admiration. It is a form of voluntary servitude, a profound belief that refuses the void and fills the fear of absence. By relinquishing their identities, the Johnnys find their reward in the gaze of others, becoming image-subjects – reflections of an icon in which reality and imagination merge. Their lives, a freely chosen sacrifice, become a form of ecstasy, perpetuating the idol’s image at the cost of their own existence. For them, imitation is a form of transcendence, a mystical quest in which appearance becomes essence. Their autonomy lies in this absolute fidelity, through which the ideal self is realised in the infinite repetition of the fixed image. Their fascination with identification anchors them in a reality where the copy becomes truer than life itself.

BB: The New Eve

Brigitte Bardot asserted a new kind of femininity, freed from the moral conventions of the post-war era. Natural and sensual, she associated desire with the freedom to choose without guilt. Simone de Beauvoir described her as an ‘Eve before original sin’, while Marguerite Duras saw her as a figure of emancipation. Her apparent innocence, combined with provocation, upended representations of femininity. Until the end of the 1960s, BB was emblematic of a modernity in which women’s autonomy asserted itself through the body as much as through attitude.

Diana and the Thirteenth Pillar

The tunnel beneath the Pont de l’Alma, on 31 August 1997, ceased to be the mere setting of an accident and became the founding site of the myth of Lady Diana, a symbolic entrance to Hades. This dark passage, a threshold to the afterlife, marks her descent into the underworld, leaving the profane world behind for a sacred realm. The absence of images of her agony, hidden away like a taboo, reinforces the mystery of a modern martyrdom bordering on sainthood, leaving room for a succession of signs and imaginary images. Her body disappears in favour of an elusive figure, preserved from all alteration, while the tunnel, a thirteenth funerary pillar, seals her passage into the invisible. The stripped wreckage releases her soul from earthly constraints, transforming the accident into a rebirth, according to a logic in which death precedes resurrection. The tunnel is therefore not an end, but a passage into eternity, where Diana, an untouchable icon, enters a world freed from human contradictions. Her Parisian martyrdom confers upon her, in the collective imagination, a form of contemporary sainthood, as a news item tips over into legend.

18 June: Speech as Act

Although the original recording of the Appeal of 18 June 1940 has been lost, it remains etched in history through a later photograph, taken on 30 October 1941, in which de Gaulle, alone before a Marconi microphone at the BBC, embodies France’s resistance. Radio, central to his strategy, enabled him to overcome his political isolation and turn words into action, despite the initial lack of understanding. Although little heard at the time, his message was relayed by the press, creating a clandestine link with the French people. Far more than a simple channel of communication, radio gave his words a unique resonance through his tone, rhythm, and silences, creating a political theatre in which each address strengthened the legitimacy of Free France. The microphone, a symbol of both his solitude and his perseverance, turned 18 June into a founding myth, far beyond its immediate impact. It became the founding act of a legitimacy – that of an ‘eternal’ France. The power of the speech lies in its performative form: words become an act that commits their speaker and brings a political reality into being, ultimately sealed by the Liberation of Paris in 1944.

Frida Kahlo, or Mexican Dolorism

Frida Kahlo’s body, marked by polio and the tram accident, became the centre of a body of work in which suffering is transformed into creation. Her dolorist imagery, inspired by Mexican ex-votos and the Passion of Christ, resonates with the figure of Saint Teresa of Ávila, for whom wounding becomes an experience of revelation. In Kahlo’s work, physical and emotional pain are transfigured into an artistic language and a means of asserting her identity. Her self-portraits and painted corsets bear witness not simply to a wounded body, but to a resistance to social and aesthetic norms. ‘Fridamania’ has helped cast Frida Kahlo as an artist-martyr, obscuring the political and subversive dimension of her work. By making the wounded body the vehicle for an unprecedented iconography, she transforms suffering into aesthetic power and an affirmation of self.

200 Years of Photography: Let’s Celebrate

From September 1, 2026, to September 30, 2027, the Ministry of Culture is organizing the Bicentennial of Photography, a major, open, and festive celebration that highlights collections, contemporary creation, photographic publishing, and the various professions within the field of photography.

Several hundred accredited events (exhibitions, symposiums, audiovisual screenings, photographic literacy projects, etc.) will take place in metropolitan France, the overseas territories, and some thirty other countries. The Bicentennial of Photography is organized by the Ministry of Culture, supported by a scientific committee chaired by Dominique de Font-Réaulx – an art historian specializing in the 19th century and photography, and chief curator at the Louvre Museum – and involving a wide range of stakeholders from the fields of culture, education, and research.

Japan’s Jimi Halloween, a celebration of all things mundane – in pictures

While Halloween is traditionally a family-oriented holiday and an occasion for children to dress up and go trick-or-treating, a unique spin on spooky season is taking off in Japan. ‘Jimi Halloween’ or ‘Mundane Halloween’ sees adult participants dress up as ordinary people in everyday life. They do highly specific tasks, embracing and celebrating unremarkable situations for the event, hosted by online magazine Daily Portal Z in Tokyo’s Shibuya district.

Tomohiro Ohsumi

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Oscar winners, Oscar nominees and Oscar hopefuls will be assembling in the UK capital next month for one of the newest film festivals on the planet.

The second edition of LDNDOCS , set to unfold from November 20-22 in central London, will present “14 new, award-winning documentary features from some of the world’s most acclaimed and exciting documentary filmmakers.” The lineup announced Tuesday boasts two-time Oscar winner Barbara Kopple, presenting her film Union Town ; Emmy winner Amir Bar-Lev with The Last First: Winter K2 ; Emmy winner Stephen Maing and Emmy nominee Eric Daniel Metzgar with The Great Experiment , and Oscar nominee Sara Dosa with her latest, Time and Water .

Scroll for the full LDNDOCS lineup.

Watch on Deadline

Oscar nominee Poh Si Teng will present her directorial debut, American Doctor , while Iranian-born director Pegah Ahangarani will screen her documentary Rehearsals for a Revolution , winner of the L’Oeil d’or prize at Cannes and recently selected as the official British entry for Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards. LDNDOCS will kick off with Once Upon a Time in Harlem , the award-winning film about an extraordinary reunion in 1972 of surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance. The documentary was conceived and shot by the late William Greaves, and realized over 50 years later by his son, David. David’s daughter Liani (William’s granddaughter) produced the film along with Anne de Mare.

Creative executive and producer Ben Fowlie ( Queer Edward II , Boatbuilders ) founded LDNDOCS. He previously founded the prestigious Camden International Film Festival in Maine, which recently held its 22nd edition. Regarding the LDNDOCS lineup, he noted, “2026 has been an incredibly exciting year for documentaries, both in terms of the range of the work and also in how nonfiction films are resonating with audiences, especially within a theatrical setting. This year’s program highlights that. It is full of bold, ambitious nonfiction films and filmmakers who are continuing to push cinematic nonfiction in new and powerful ways.”

Screenings for LDNDOCS will take place at the Curzon Bloomsbury Cinema, Bertha DocHouse, and Garden Cinema and will be followed by discussions with the visiting directors and special guests. LDNDOCS says its mission “is simple: to bring extraordinary stories to the big screen, because we believe the future of cinema is cinema. Our goal is to help the documentary form thrive, building audiences one screening at a time.”

This is the 2026 lineup for LDNDOCS:

American Doctor

Directed by Poh Si Teng | USA, State of Palestine, Malaysia, Qatar, Denmark | 2026 | 93 min

Three American medics return home from working in hospitals in Gaza, determined to fight for the patients and colleagues they left behind.

Bleeding Hearts

Directed by Andrew Morgan | USA | 2026 | 97 min

A music-driven love story about real-life couple Zella Day and Jesse Woods, two musicians chasing a shared dream while navigating pressures that could spark their breakup—or their breakthrough.

A Fox Under A Pink Moon

Directed by Mehrdad Oskouei and Soraya Akhalaghi | Iran, France | 2025 | 76 min

Five years, one smartphone, two directors — a long-distance self-portrait of an emigrant’s journey.

The Great Experiment

Directed by Stephen Maing and Eric Daniel Metzgar | USA | 2025 | 100 min

THE GREAT EXPERIMENT is an epic poem in documentary form – a mirror held to a nation at war with its own reflection, asking not who is right, but whether the experiment itself can survive.‍

The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer

Directed by Alessandra Sanguinetti | Argentina | 2026 | 96 min

Spanning more than 20 years, this intimate portrait of two girls, their everyday lives, fantasies and dreams explores their realities and inequalities of growing up female in rural Argentina.

Jean-Michel Basquiat

Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman | USA | 2026 | 95 min

Through untold memories from close friends and family and rare archival imagery, this film demystifies the story of Basquiat and discovers the man behind it all, Jean-Michel.

Khosha: The New Land

Directed by Gakemotho Satau and Zander Booth | Botswana, USA | 2026 | 67 min

Near the beautiful and mysterious Okavango Delta in the heart of Africa, eight members of the Khwe Bushman tribe – descendants of the oldest living human culture – embark on a long journey to find a new homeland.

The Last First: Winter K2

Directed by Amir Bar-Lev | USA, UK | 2026 | 98 min

A historic race to become the first to summit K2 in winter unravels into tragedy, exposing how ambition, ego, and the pursuit of glory can be as dangerous as the mountain itself.

Nuisance Bear

Directed by Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman | USA | 2026 | 90 min

A polar bear is forced to navigate a human world of tourists, wildlife officers, and hunters as its ancient migration collides with modern life. When a sacred predator is branded a nuisance, it becomes unclear who truly belongs in this shared landscape.

Once Upon A Time in Harlem

Directed by David Greaves | USA | 2026 | 100 min

A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance.

Rehearsals for a Revolution

Directed by Pegah Ahangarani | USA | 2026 | 95 min

Through five portraits of relatives and mentors, five expressions of resistance, Pegah Ahangarani sketches her life story. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protests footage, newspapers, and recorded voices, she retraces more than 40 years of Iran’s history.

To Hold A Mountain

Directed by Biljana Tuturov and Petar Glomazić | Serbia, France, Montenegro, Slovenia, Croatia| 2026 | 82 min

In the remote highlands of Montenegro, a shepherd mother and daughter proudly defend their ancestral mountain from the threat of becoming a NATO military training ground, stirring memories of the violence that shattered their family.

Time and Water

Directed by Sara Dosa | USA, Iceland | 2026 | 90 min

Facing the death of his country’s glaciers and the loss of his beloved grandparents, Icelandic writer Andri Snær Magnason turns his archives into a time capsule to hold what is slipping away — family, memory, time, and water.

Union Town

Directed by Barbara Kopple | USA | 2025 | 106 min UNION TOWN completes Barbara Kopple’s trilogy on labor rights following her Oscar-winning HARLAN COUNTY, USA and AMERICAN DREAM, two landmark cinéma vérité documentaries.
